claim: Recent genomic and scRNA-seq analyses of melanoma demonstrated a lack of recurrent genetic drivers of metastasis.
source: Recent genomic and scRNA-seq analyses of melanoma demonstrated a lack of recurrent genetic drivers of metastasis, while identifying common transcriptional states correlating with invasion or drug resistance.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to published literature on melanoma genomic and transcriptional analyses.

claim: Recent genomic and scRNA-seq analyses of melanoma identified common transcriptional states correlating with invasion or drug resistance.
source: Recent genomic and scRNA-seq analyses of melanoma demonstrated a lack of recurrent genetic drivers of metastasis, while identifying common transcriptional states correlating with invasion or drug resistance.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to published literature on melanoma transcriptional states.

claim: The zebrafish mitfa:BRAFV600E;tp53-/- melanoma model is characterized by minimal genetic evolution during malignant progression.
source: To test whether transcriptional adaptation can drive melanoma progression, we made use of a zebrafish mitfa:BRAFV600E;tp53-/- model, in which malignant progression is characterized by minimal genetic evolution.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' characterization of their zebrafish model system.

claim: An overexpression-screen of 80 epigenetic/transcriptional regulators was performed in the zebrafish melanoma model.
source: We undertook an overexpression-screen of 80 epigenetic/transcriptional regulators and found neural crest-mesenchyme developmental regulator SATB2 to accelerate aggressive melanoma development.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: SATB2 accelerates aggressive melanoma development in the zebrafish model.
source: We undertook an overexpression-screen of 80 epigenetic/transcriptional regulators and found neural crest-mesenchyme developmental regulator SATB2 to accelerate aggressive melanoma development.
evidence: This claim is supported by the screening data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SATB2 overexpression induces invadopodia formation in zebrafish tumors.
source: Its overexpression induces invadopodia formation and invasion in zebrafish tumors and human melanoma cell lines.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on invadopodia formation.

claim: SATB2 overexpression induces invasion in zebrafish tumors.
source: Its overexpression induces invadopodia formation and invasion in zebrafish tumors and human melanoma cell lines.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on tumor invasion.

claim: SATB2 overexpression induces invadopodia formation in human melanoma cell lines.
source: Its overexpression induces invadopodia formation and invasion in zebrafish tumors and human melanoma cell lines.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on human cell lines.

claim: SATB2 overexpression induces invasion in human melanoma cell lines.
source: Its overexpression induces invadopodia formation and invasion in zebrafish tumors and human melanoma cell lines.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on human cell lines.

claim: SATB2 binds neural crest-regulators including pdgfab.
source: SATB2 binds and activates neural crest-regulators, including pdgfab and snai2.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SATB2 binds neural crest-regulators including snai2.
source: SATB2 binds and activates neural crest-regulators, including pdgfab and snai2.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SATB2 activates neural crest-regulators including pdgfab.
source: SATB2 binds and activates neural crest-regulators, including pdgfab and snai2.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: SATB2 activates neural crest-regulators including snai2.
source: SATB2 binds and activates neural crest-regulators, including pdgfab and snai2.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: The transcriptional program induced by SATB2 overlaps with the MITFlowAXLhigh drug-resistant state.
source: The transcriptional program induced by SATB2 overlaps with known MITFlowAXLhigh and AQP1+NGFR1high drug-resistant states and functionally drives enhanced tumor propagation and resistance to Vemurafenib in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis comparing SATB2-induced transcriptional changes with published signatures.

claim: The transcriptional program induced by SATB2 overlaps with the AQP1+NGFR1high drug-resistant state.
source: The transcriptional program induced by SATB2 overlaps with known MITFlowAXLhigh and AQP1+NGFR1high drug-resistant states and functionally drives enhanced tumor propagation and resistance to Vemurafenib in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis comparing SATB2-induced transcriptional changes with published signatures.

claim: SATB2 functionally drives enhanced tumor propagation in vivo.
source: The transcriptional program induced by SATB2 overlaps with known MITFlowAXLhigh and AQP1+NGFR1high drug-resistant states and functionally drives enhanced tumor propagation and resistance to Vemurafenib in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by limiting dilution transplantation experiments.

claim: SATB2 functionally drives resistance to Vemurafenib in vivo.
source: The transcriptional program induced by SATB2 overlaps with known MITFlowAXLhigh and AQP1+NGFR1high drug-resistant states and functionally drives enhanced tumor propagation and resistance to Vemurafenib in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo drug treatment experiments.

claim: Acquisition of oncogenic BRAF or NRAS mutations alone is insufficient to drive melanoma initiation.
source: Both sequencing of patient precursor lesions (Shain et al., 2015) and modeling in transgenic animals (Pérez-Guijarro et al., 2017; van Rooijen et al., 2017) showed that acquisition of oncogenic BRAF or NRAS mutations alone is insufficient to drive melanoma initiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by cited studies on patient samples and animal models.

claim: Few driver mutations are acquired in early transformed melanocytes.
source: Reconstruction of the clonal history of advanced human melanoma suggests that few driver mutations, including loss of tumor suppressors, are acquired in early transformed melanocytes, and that high mutational burden and genomic instability are later events in malignant progression (Birkeland et al., 2018; Ding et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by cited clonal history studies.

claim: High mutational burden and genomic instability are later events in melanoma malignant progression.
source: Reconstruction of the clonal history of advanced human melanoma suggests that few driver mutations, including loss of tumor suppressors, are acquired in early transformed melanocytes, and that high mutational burden and genomic instability are later events in malignant progression (Birkeland et al., 2018; Ding et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by cited clonal history studies.

claim: Metastatic melanoma tumors show a high degree of similarity in mutational landscape and driver genes compared to their respective primaries.
source: Recently, a pan-cancer whole-genome analysis of metastatic solid tumors, including 248 melanoma patients, showed a surprisingly high degree of similarity in mutational landscape and driver genes between metastatic tumors and their respective primaries, as well as across multiple metastatic lesions within the same patient (Priestley et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a cited pan-cancer genomic analysis.

claim: Multiple metastatic lesions within the same melanoma patient show limited genetic diversity.
source: Recently, a pan-cancer whole-genome analysis of metastatic solid tumors, including 248 melanoma patients, showed a surprisingly high degree of similarity in mutational landscape and driver genes between metastatic tumors and their respective primaries, as well as across multiple metastatic lesions within the same patient (Priestley et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a cited pan-cancer genomic analysis.

claim: Genetic selection of mutated drivers is unlikely to be responsible for metastatic progression in melanoma.
source: The lack of recurrently mutated genes in metastasis, and the limited genetic diversity across metastatic sites suggests that genetic selection of mutated drivers is unlikely to be responsible for metastatic progression.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the cited genomic data.

claim: Bulk RNA-seq and scRNA-seq analyses of metastatic melanoma have identified common recurrent transcriptional states correlating with invasion.
source: Meanwhile, despite the high degree of mutational burden and genetic intra- and inter-patient heterogeneity observed in melanoma, several bulk RNA-seq and scRNA-seq analyses of metastatic melanoma patient samples have identified common recurrent transcriptional states correlating with invasion (mesenchymal signature; Verfaillie et al., 2015), drug resistance (MITFlow/AXLhigh; Tirosh et al., 2016), a neural crest-like state correlating with minimal residual disease persistence during targeted therapy with MAPK inhibitors (MITFlow/NGFR1high/AQP1high; Rambow et al., 2018), and even response to immunotherapy (NGFR1high; Boshuizen et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by cited RNA-seq studies.

claim: A MITFlow/AXLhigh transcriptional state correlates with drug resistance in melanoma.
source: Meanwhile, despite the high degree of mutational burden and genetic intra- and inter-patient heterogeneity observed in melanoma, several bulk RNA-seq and scRNA-seq analyses of metastatic melanoma patient samples have identified common recurrent transcriptional states correlating with invasion (mesenchymal signature; Verfaillie et al., 2015), drug resistance (MITFlow/AXLhigh; Tirosh et al., 2016), a neural crest-like state correlating with minimal residual disease persistence during targeted therapy with MAPK inhibitors (MITFlow/NGFR1high/AQP1high; Rambow et al., 2018), and even response to immunotherapy (NGFR1high; Boshuizen et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a cited scRNA-seq study.

claim: A neural crest-like MITFlow/NGFR1high/AQP1high state correlates with minimal residual disease persistence during targeted therapy with MAPK inhibitors.
source: Meanwhile, despite the high degree of mutational burden and genetic intra- and inter-patient heterogeneity observed in melanoma, several bulk RNA-seq and scRNA-seq analyses of metastatic melanoma patient samples have identified common recurrent transcriptional states correlating with invasion (mesenchymal signature; Verfaillie et al., 2015), drug resistance (MITFlow/AXLhigh; Tirosh et al., 2016), a neural crest-like state correlating with minimal residual disease persistence during targeted therapy with MAPK inhibitors (MITFlow/NGFR1high/AQP1high; Rambow et al., 2018), and even response to immunotherapy (NGFR1high; Boshuizen et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a cited study on melanoma transcriptional states.

claim: A NGFR1high transcriptional state correlates with response to immunotherapy in melanoma.
source: Meanwhile, despite the high degree of mutational burden and genetic intra- and inter-patient heterogeneity observed in melanoma, several bulk RNA-seq and scRNA-seq analyses of metastatic melanoma patient samples have identified common recurrent transcriptional states correlating with invasion (mesenchymal signature; Verfaillie et al., 2015), drug resistance (MITFlow/AXLhigh; Tirosh et al., 2016), a neural crest-like state correlating with minimal residual disease persistence during targeted therapy with MAPK inhibitors (MITFlow/NGFR1high/AQP1high; Rambow et al., 2018), and even response to immunotherapy (NGFR1high; Boshuizen et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a cited study on immunotherapy response.

claim: In a zebrafish transgenic melanoma model, only a few cells or subclones from a cancerized field of melanocytes carrying driving oncogenic mutations will develop a malignant tumor.
source: Using a zebrafish transgenic melanoma model, we have previously shown that in a cancerized field of melanocytes carrying driving oncogenic mutations, such as BRAFV600E and loss of tp53, only a few cells or subclones will go on to develop a malignant tumor, and that this event is marked by re-expression of developmental neural crest (NC)markers sox10 and crestin (Kaufman et al., 2016; McConnell et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by cited previous work from the authors' group.

claim: Malignant tumor development in zebrafish melanoma is marked by re-expression of developmental neural crest markers sox10 and crestin.
source: Using a zebrafish transgenic melanoma model, we have previously shown that in a cancerized field of melanocytes carrying driving oncogenic mutations, such as BRAFV600E and loss of tp53, only a few cells or subclones will go on to develop a malignant tumor, and that this event is marked by re-expression of developmental neural crest (NC)markers sox10 and crestin (Kaufman et al., 2016; McConnell et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by cited previous work from the authors' group.

claim: Malignant progression from transformed melanocytes in experimental animal models is not explained by the very limited genetic evolution observed in these tumors.
source: Similar to the observation in human metastatic patient samples, malignant progression from transformed melanocytes in experimental animal models is not explained by the very limited genetic evolution observed in these tumors (Yen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a cited study on genetic evolution in animal models.

claim: SATB2 acts as a transcriptional regulator by recruiting members of the acetyl transferase and histone demethylase complexes to target genes.
source: SATB2 acts as a transcriptional regulator by recruiting members of the acetyl transferase and histone demethylase complexes to target genes and altering the local chromatin organization and activation state (Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a cited study on SATB2 function.

claim: SATB2 alters local chromatin organization and activation state.
source: SATB2 acts as a transcriptional regulator by recruiting members of the acetyl transferase and histone demethylase complexes to target genes and altering the local chromatin organization and activation state (Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a cited study on SATB2 function.

claim: SATB2 expression correlates with patient outcome in several tumor types.
source: Its expression has been shown to correlate with patient outcome in several tumor types (Naik and Galande, 2019; Yu et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by cited studies on SATB2 in cancer.

claim: SATB2 plays a role in oncogenic transformation and proliferation in different tissues and tumor types.
source: In different tissues and tumor types, SATB2 has been shown to play a role in oncogenic transformation and proliferation, or epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), migration, and self-renewal (Gan et al., 2017; Naik and Galande, 2019; Nayak et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2017a).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple cited studies on SATB2 in cancer.

claim: SATB2 plays a role in epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), migration, and self-renewal in different tissues and tumor types.
source: In different tissues and tumor types, SATB2 has been shown to play a role in oncogenic transformation and proliferation, or epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), migration, and self-renewal (Gan et al., 2017; Naik and Galande, 2019; Nayak et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2017a).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple cited studies on SATB2 in cancer.

claim: SATB2 has a well-conserved structure and expression pattern across chicken, mouse, and zebrafish during development and migration of the cranial neural crest.
source: SATB2 is a transcription factor and chromatin remodeler with a well-conserved structure and expression pattern across chicken, mouse, and zebrafish during the development and migration of the cranial neural crest (CNC) and neuronal development.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge of SATB2 in developmental biology.

claim: SATB2 is required for the development of the exo-mesenchymal lineages of the cranial neural crest.
source: It is required for the development of the exo-mesenchymal lineages of the CNC (Sheehan-Rooney et al., 2010; Sheehan-Rooney et al., 2013), and neuronal axon formation (McKenna et al., 2015; Shinmyo and Kawasaki, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by cited developmental biology studies.

claim: SATB2 is required for neuronal axon formation.
source: It is required for the development of the exo-mesenchymal lineages of the CNC (Sheehan-Rooney et al., 2010; Sheehan-Rooney et al., 2013), and neuronal axon formation (McKenna et al., 2015; Shinmyo and Kawasaki, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by cited developmental biology studies.

claim: SATB2 inactivating mutations in humans are associated with cleft palate, intellectual disability, facial dysmorphism, and development of odontomas.
source: In facts, SATB2 inactivating mutations in humans have been associated with cleft palate, intellectual disability, facial dysmorphism, and development of odontomas, defining a neurocristopathy referred to as SATB2-associated syndrome (Kikuiri et al., 2018; Zarate et al., 2019; Zarate and Fish, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by cited clinical studies on SATB2 syndrome.

claim: SATB2 drives enhanced invasion via invadopodia formation in zebrafish in vivo allotransplants.
source: Through a combination of zebrafish in vivo allotransplants and validation in human melanoma cell lines, we show that SATB2 drives enhanced invasion via invadopodia formation and an EMT-like phenotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from zebrafish transplantation experiments.

claim: SATB2 drives an EMT-like phenotype in zebrafish in vivo allotransplants.
source: Through a combination of zebrafish in vivo allotransplants and validation in human melanoma cell lines, we show that SATB2 drives enhanced invasion via invadopodia formation and an EMT-like phenotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from zebrafish transplantation experiments.

claim: SATB2 drives enhanced invasion via invadopodia formation in human melanoma cell lines.
source: Through a combination of zebrafish in vivo allotransplants and validation in human melanoma cell lines, we show that SATB2 drives enhanced invasion via invadopodia formation and an EMT-like phenotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from human cell line studies.

claim: SATB2 drives an EMT-like phenotype in human melanoma cell lines.
source: Through a combination of zebrafish in vivo allotransplants and validation in human melanoma cell lines, we show that SATB2 drives enhanced invasion via invadopodia formation and an EMT-like phenotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from human cell line studies.

claim: Chromatin and transcriptional characterization of primary zebrafish SATB2 tumors vs. EGFP controls was performed via ChIP-seq and RNA-seq.
source: Mechanistically, chromatin and transcriptional characterization of primary zebrafish SATB2 tumors vs. EGFP controls via ChIP-seq and RNA-seq shows SATB2 to bind and induce transcriptional activation of neural crest regulators, including snai2 and pdgfab.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: The transcriptional program induced by SATB2 overexpression is conserved between zebrafish and human melanoma.
source: The transcriptional program induced by SATB2 overexpression is conserved between zebrafish and human melanoma, and overlaps with the aforementioned MITFlow/AXLhigh (Tirosh et al., 2016) and neural crest-like MITFlow/NGFR1high/AQP1high drug-resistant states (Rambow et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative RNA-seq analysis between zebrafish and human melanoma.

claim: Pool F had the strongest acceleration phenotype in the melanoma screen.
source: We identified six significant candidate accelerator pools (Pool B,D,F,G,I,L vs. MCR:EGFP Log-rank (Mantel-Cox) test p<0.0001****) of which Pool F had the strongest acceleration (Figure 1B), and tested individual factors from four accelerating pools (B/F/G/I) and a non-significant pool (C) (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the Kaplan-Meier survival data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: SATB2-overexpression accelerates melanoma development with a median onset of 12 weeks compared to 21.4 weeks for MCR:EGFP.
source: Single factor validation of Pool F (Figure 1C) showed that SATB2-overexpression (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B) is sufficient to strongly accelerate melanoma development (median onset of 12 weeks, compared to 21.4 weeks for MCR:EGFP, Log-rank (Mantel-Cox) test p<0.0001****) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the Kaplan-Meier survival data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: MCR:SATB2 tumors appear grossly aggressive.
source: MCR:SATB2 tumors appear grossly aggressive (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, Video 1), are invasive, and melanoma cells are frequently observed in internal organs and spreading along the spinal cord, while organ involvement is rarely observed in MCR:EGFP (Figure 1E–G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by gross anatomical observations shown in Figure 1D and supplementary figures.

claim: MCR:SATB2 tumors are invasive.
source: MCR:SATB2 tumors appear grossly aggressive (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, Video 1), are invasive, and melanoma cells are frequently observed in internal organs and spreading along the spinal cord, while organ involvement is rarely observed in MCR:EGFP (Figure 1E–G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by histopathological analysis shown in Figure 1E-G.

claim: Melanoma cells in MCR:SATB2 tumors are frequently observed in internal organs.
source: MCR:SATB2 tumors appear grossly aggressive (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, Video 1), are invasive, and melanoma cells are frequently observed in internal organs and spreading along the spinal cord, while organ involvement is rarely observed in MCR:EGFP (Figure 1E–G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by histopathological analysis shown in Figure 1E-G.

claim: Melanoma cells in MCR:SATB2 tumors are frequently observed spreading along the spinal cord.
source: MCR:SATB2 tumors appear grossly aggressive (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, Video 1), are invasive, and melanoma cells are frequently observed in internal organs and spreading along the spinal cord, while organ involvement is rarely observed in MCR:EGFP (Figure 1E–G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by histopathological analysis shown in Figure 1E-G.

claim: Organ involvement is rarely observed in MCR:EGFP tumors.
source: MCR:SATB2 tumors appear grossly aggressive (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, Video 1), are invasive, and melanoma cells are frequently observed in internal organs and spreading along the spinal cord, while organ involvement is rarely observed in MCR:EGFP (Figure 1E–G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by histopathological analysis shown in Figure 1E-G.

claim: SATB2 effect on melanoma development is BRAFV600E and tp53-/- dependent.
source: SATB2 effect on melanoma development is BRAFV600E and tp53-/-dependent (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic dependency experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Melanocyte-specific expression of Cas9 and a gRNA targeting zebrafish satb2 did not affect tumor onset compared to control targeting tp53.
source: Melanocyte-specific expression of Cas9 and of a gRNA efficiently targeting zebrafish satb2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B) using the established MCR:CRISPR system (Ablain et al., 2018) did not affect tumor onset compared to control targeting tp53 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by CRISPR knockout experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: satb2 is likely dispensable for melanoma initiation.
source: While we did not verify satb2 expression in transgenic tumors, this data suggest it to likely be dispensable for melanoma initiation.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the CRISPR knockout data.

claim: SATB1 did not affect tumor development.
source: Furthermore, SATB2 closely related gene SATB1 did not affect tumor development (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by overexpression experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D.

claim: SATB2-overexpression in primary zebrafish tumors did not result in increased proliferation.
source: The acceleration phenotype is not due to increased cellular proliferation, since SATB2-overexpression in primary zebrafish tumors (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A) or in a panel of human melanoma cell lines via a TETon tetracycline inducible lentiviral vector (here referred to as iSATB2) did not result in increased proliferation (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by proliferation assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: SATB2-overexpression in a panel of human melanoma cell lines did not result in increased proliferation.
source: The acceleration phenotype is not due to increased cellular proliferation, since SATB2-overexpression in primary zebrafish tumors (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A) or in a panel of human melanoma cell lines via a TETon tetracycline inducible lentiviral vector (here referred to as iSATB2) did not result in increased proliferation (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by proliferation assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B,C.

claim: SATB2-overexpression accelerates melanoma malignant progression without affecting proliferation.
source: Our data demonstrate that SATB2-overexpression accelerates melanoma malignant progression without affecting proliferation, but SATB2 is not sufficient and unlikely to be required for melanoma initiation.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the experimental findings on SATB2 effects.

claim: SATB2 is not sufficient for melanoma initiation.
source: Our data demonstrate that SATB2-overexpression accelerates melanoma malignant progression without affecting proliferation, but SATB2 is not sufficient and unlikely to be required for melanoma initiation.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental data showing SATB2 requires BRAF and p53 mutations.

claim: SATB2 is unlikely to be required for melanoma initiation.
source: Our data demonstrate that SATB2-overexpression accelerates melanoma malignant progression without affecting proliferation, but SATB2 is not sufficient and unlikely to be required for melanoma initiation.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the CRISPR knockout data.

claim: Primary zebrafish melanoma in vitro cell cultures showed heightened migration potential in MCR:SATB2 cell lines compared to MCR:EGFP cell lines.
source: Using primary zebrafish melanoma in vitro cell cultures, we performed scratch migration assays, that confirmed a heightened migration potential of 3 independent MCR:SATB2 cell lines compared to three independent MCR:EGFP cell lines (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by scratch assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cytoskeletal staining of zebrafish melanoma in vitro cultures revealed the presence of strong F-actin-positive foci in MCR:SATB2 cells.
source: Cytoskeletal staining of zebrafish melanoma in vitro cultures (Zmel1 MCR:EGFP and 45–3 MCR:SATB2) with phalloidin revealed the presence of strong F-actin-positive foci in MCR:SATB2 cells (Figure 2A), reminiscent of invadopodia.
evidence: This claim is supported by phalloidin staining data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Invadopodia are cell protrusions involved in metastatic spreading by facilitating anchorage of cells to, and local degradation of the ECM.
source: Invadopodia are cell protrusions involved in metastatic spreading by facilitating anchorage of cells to, and local degradation of the ECM (Murphy and Courtneidge, 2011), and are known to be regulated by the PDGF-SRC pathway and EMT.
evidence: This claim is supported by cited literature on invadopodia.

claim: Invadopodia are known to be regulated by the PDGF-SRC pathway and EMT.
source: Invadopodia are cell protrusions involved in metastatic spreading by facilitating anchorage of cells to, and local degradation of the ECM (Murphy and Courtneidge, 2011), and are known to be regulated by the PDGF-SRC pathway and EMT.
evidence: This claim is supported by cited literature on invadopodia regulation.

claim: During normal development, invadopodia-like physiologically equivalent structures called podosomes are utilized by neural crest cells to migrate.
source: During normal development, invadopodia-like physiologically equivalent structures called podosomes are utilized by neural crest cells to migrate (Murphy and Courtneidge, 2011; Murphy et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by cited literature on neural crest cell migration.

claim: Co-localization of F-actin with Cortactin in MCR:SATB2 melanoma cell lines confirmed these foci to be invadopodia.
source: Co-localization of F-actin with invadopodium structural component Cortactin in MCR:SATB2 melanoma cell lines confirmed these foci to be invadopodia (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Primary MCR:SATB2 tumors showed abundant Cortactin expression compared to MCR:EGFP.
source: Much like in vitro cultures, primary MCR:SATB2 tumors also showed abundant Cortactin expression compared to MCR:EGFP (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: MCR:SATB2 melanoma cell lines strongly degraded the gelatin matrix, with 49.2–57.9% of cells having degraded gelatin, compared to 5.4% of MCR:Empty control cells.
source: MCR:SATB2 melanoma cell lines strongly degraded the gelatin matrix, with 49.2–57.9% of cells having degraded gelatin, compared to 5.4% of MCR:Empty control cells (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by gelatin degradation assay data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D.

claim: Upon SATB2 induction, all human melanoma cell lines robustly formed invadopodia and showed significantly increased matrix degradation.
source: Upon SATB2 induction (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B), all human melanoma cell lines robustly formed invadopodia and showed significantly increased matrix degradation (Figure 2D–E, Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by gelatin degradation assay data shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: In SKMEL2, a 10-fold induction of cells with matrix degradation was observed, from a baseline of 5.4 ± 4.5% (SD) to 58.2 ± 13.2% (SD) after doxycycline treatment.
source: In SKMEL2, a 10-fold induction of cells with matrix degradation was observed, from a baseline of 5.4 ± 4.5% (SD) of cells with matrix degradation to 58.2 ± 13.2% (SD) of cells after doxycycline treatment (Figure 2D–E), with evidence of F-actin and Cortactin co-localization in punctae below the cell nucleus, characteristic of invadopodia (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative gelatin degradation assay data shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: 59.4 ± 2.3% (SEM; n = 76 total recipients, grafted from seven individual donor tumors) of MCR:SATB2 transplants formed distant metastasis, compared to 21.8±4.5% (SEM; n = 37 total recipients grafted from five individual donor tumors) of EGFP-control transplants.
source: Pooled recipient data at the experimental end point at 3.5 weeks post-transplantation, 59.4 ± 2.3% (SEM; n = 76 total recipients, grafted from seven individual donor tumors) of MCR:SATB2 transplants formed distant metastasis, compared to 21.8±4.5% (SEM; n = 37 total recipients grafted from five individual donor tumors) of EGFP-control transplants (p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of transplantation experiments.

claim: MCR:EGFP transplants developed an average 1.1 ± 0.4 (SD) distant metastasis per fish, versus 4 ± 4.2 (SD) in MCR:SATB2, where a maximum of 20 metastases per fish was observed.
source: MCR:EGFP transplants developed an average 1.1 ± 0.4 (SD) distant metastasis per fish, versus 4 ± 4.2 (SD) in MCR:SATB2, where a maximum of 20 metastases per fish was observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of metastasis numbers in transplantation experiments.

claim: MCR:SATB2 recipients more frequently developed bilateral metastases (28.9% versus 5.4% in MCR:EGFP).
source: MCR:SATB2 recipients more frequently developed bilateral (28.9%), and internal metastases (22.4%) compared to MCR:EGFP donors (5.4%), showing spreading along the neural tube (14.5% versus 2.7%).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of metastasis patterns in transplantation experiments.

claim: MCR:SATB2 recipients more frequently developed internal metastases (22.4% versus 5.4% in MCR:EGFP).
source: MCR:SATB2 recipients more frequently developed bilateral (28.9%), and internal metastases (22.4%) compared to MCR:EGFP donors (5.4%), showing spreading along the neural tube (14.5% versus 2.7%).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of metastasis patterns in transplantation experiments.

claim: MCR:SATB2 recipients showed spreading along the neural tube (14.5% versus 2.7% in MCR:EGFP).
source: MCR:SATB2 recipients more frequently developed bilateral (28.9%), and internal metastases (22.4%) compared to MCR:EGFP donors (5.4%), showing spreading along the neural tube (14.5% versus 2.7%).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of metastasis patterns in transplantation experiments.

claim: SATB2 is endogenously expressed in human melanoma at the RNA level.
source: SATB2 is endogenously expressed in human melanoma at the RNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A) and protein level (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: SATB2 is endogenously expressed in human melanoma at the protein level.
source: SATB2 is endogenously expressed in human melanoma at the RNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A) and protein level (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by protein expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: SATB2 is infrequently but recurrently amplified in ~4–8% of metastatic melanoma patients.

claim: satb2 is highly expressed in a published dataset of migrating crestin:EGFP+-NC cells sorted from zebrafish embryos at the 15 somite stage.

claim: Both Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) Hallmark pathways analysis and Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA) showed similar effects of SATB2 overexpression between the human melanoma cell line (SKMEL2 iSATB2) and zebrafish tumors (MCR:SATB2 vs. EGFP).

claim: GSEA analysis in SKMEL2 iSATB2 showed a significant overlap of the SATB2-induced transcriptional program with the less differentiated MITFlow/AXLhigh state (NES = 1.54, p=0.000, q = 0.17).
